text.p: Texaco Inc made "significant strides" toward the goals of its diversity plan during the first six months of a five-year effort, Chief Executive Officer Peter Bijur said Tuesday.
"Last December, Texaco made a commitment to a more inclusive and diverse workforce and to broader relationships with women- and minority-owned businesses," said Bijur.
"The momentum we created in the first half of the year is a strong beginning for this program," he continued.
During the period, 50 percent of the about 4,400 new hires in the U.S. were women and 38 percent were minorities.
Texaco said African-Americans accounted for 16 percent of the hires and Hispanics accounted for 15 percent.
To enhance recruitment, search firms were asked to identify a wider array of candidates, and Texaco's recruitment programs were expanded to include more minority colleges.

Texaco said women earned 47 percent of the about 325 promotions during the first six months of the year and minorities earned 24 percent, including 12 percent by African- Americans and eight percent by Hispanics. Written leadership standards were completed to identify development needs of managers and to select leaders for promotion, it said.
A new training program for first-time managers and supervisors is now being piloted, Texaco said.
It said all U.S. employees must participate in a redesigned two-day diversity learning experience.
All human resource committee meetings held in each business unit now include representation by women and minorities.
Texaco's expanded 360-degree feedback program is being implemented to provide each manager with an annual review by their direct reports, peers and their own manager.

Managers' success in meeting inclusive workforce goals is tied to their compensation and performance reviews. Also, executive compensation is now linked to the achievement of inclusive workforce goals and to annual employee survey results relating to respect for the individual.
Through June 30, direct expenditures with minority- and women-owned businesses increased $37 million over the same period in 1996 to $106 million, Texaco said.
In addition to the $106 million, more than $1 million in service fees were paid to minority- and women-owned financial services firms during the first half of 1997.
Purchases from African-American and Hispanic firms totaled about $8 million each, up respectively from $1.6 million and $5 million in 1996.

Texaco now retains 21 minority- or women-owned law firms and two minority advertising agencies, up from six and zero respectively in 1996. The use of minorities also increased in accounting, tax, public relations and human resources.
Texaco said more than 50 banking relationships with minority and women firms are in place, versus 21 in 1996.
Investments handled by minority and women pension managers increased to $186 million from $31 million in 1996.
A new venture capital investment of $5 million was implemented with a minority-owned business.
A group of minority- and women-owned firms underwrote a $150 million public financing for Texaco, it said, adding this was a first for a U.S. industrial company.
Insurance coverage with an African-American-owned company increased to $200 million from $25 million.
Texaco said it added eight minority and women wholesalers, ahead of schedule to add nine in its full-year 1997 plan.
Three African-American retailers were added in the first half of the year. Five Star Mart Franchise agreements were signed with minorities, one of which was African American.
Overall, the company said, it is committed to maintaining the level of women and minority independent retail owners and lessee operators at the existing 45 percent level.
This commitment was made when the diversity program was announced in mid-December, a month after the big oil company agreed to settle a class action lawsuit filed in 1994 by 1,440 black employees.

The settlement, which included a $115 million payment to the plaintiffs and an 11 percent salary increase for those still employed by Texaco, followed release of a tape recording of company executives discussing the case. The tape was made by one of the participants who was later fired by Texaco.

Texaco said the level of minority and women managers at company owned and operated retail outlets is 67 percent. Texaco added 12 African-American store managers in the first six months, far exceeding its full-year goal of adding eight.
Seven minority- and women-owned Xpress Lube outlets opened, ahead of the schedule to achieve 10 in the full-year plan. ((-- New York Newsdesk 212 859-1610))
